title: How do you write a production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app (multi-stage build, layered JAR for cache efficiency, slim JRE base, non-root user, `MaxRAMPercentage`), and why does instruction order matter for layer caching?
shortTitle: Writing a production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app — multi-stage, layered JAR, slim JRE, non-root, MaxRAMPercentage, and why instruction order matters

s1_definition.profdef: A production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application uses a multi-stage build so the heavy build toolchain (JDK, Maven) stays in a throwaway builder stage and only the compiled artifact lands in a small runtime image. It unpacks the Spring Boot fat JAR into Spring's layered format so Docker can cache the rarely-changing dependency layers separately from the frequently-changing application-code layer. It runs on a slim JRE base image rather than a full JDK, runs as a non-root user for security, and passes `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` so the JVM sizes its heap as a percentage of the container's memory limit instead of the host's. Instruction order matters because Docker builds images as a stack of cached layers, and any instruction that changes invalidates that layer and every layer after it, so you place the things that change least (dependencies) before the things that change most (your code).
s1_definition.analogy: Think of building the National Bank of India's mobile banking app container like preparing a secure cash-delivery van for the street. The multi-stage build is like assembling the van in a fully-equipped workshop (all the welding tools, the JDK, Maven) but sending only the finished van out — you do not drive the entire workshop around the city. The layered JAR is like packing the van so the heavy, rarely-changing equipment (third-party libraries) goes in first and the daily paperwork (your application code) goes in a top drawer you can swap without repacking the whole van. The slim JRE is a lean van with only what it needs to run, not a mobile workshop. Running as non-root is giving the driver only the keys to the van, not the master key to the whole depot. And `MaxRAMPercentage` tells the van how much of ITS OWN fuel tank to use, rather than assuming it has the whole depot's fuel supply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Build in a throwaway JDK stage, ship a slim JRE image with layered dependencies cached below your code, run as non-root, and let `MaxRAMPercentage` size the heap to the container — order instructions least-changing first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application uses a multi-stage build so the heavy build toolchain (JDK, Maven) stays in a throwaway builder stage and only the compiled artifact lands in a small runtime image. It unpacks the Spring Boot fat JAR into Spring's layered format so Docker can cache the rarely-changing dependency layers separately from the frequently-changing application-code layer. It runs on a slim JRE base image rather than a full JDK, runs as a non-root user for security, and passes `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` so the JVM sizes its heap as a percentage of the container's memory limit instead of the host's. Instruction order matters because Docker builds images as a stack of cached layers, and any instruction that changes invalidates that layer and every layer after it, so you place the things that change least (dependencies) before the things that change most (your code).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of building the National Bank of India's mobile banking app container like preparing a secure cash-delivery van for the street. The multi-stage build is like assembling the van in a fully-equipped workshop (all the welding tools, the JDK, Maven) but sending only the finished van out — you do not drive the entire workshop around the city. The layered JAR is like packing the van so the heavy, rarely-changing equipment (third-party libraries) goes in first and the daily paperwork (your application code) goes in a top drawer you can swap without repacking the whole van. The slim JRE is a lean van with only what it needs to run, not a mobile workshop. Running as non-root is giving the driver only the keys to the van, not the master key to the whole depot. And `MaxRAMPercentage` tells the van how much of ITS OWN fuel tank to use, rather than assuming it has the whole depot's fuel supply.

**One line to remember:** Build in a throwaway JDK stage, ship a slim JRE image with layered dependencies cached below your code, run as non-root, and let `MaxRAMPercentage` size the heap to the container — order instructions least-changing first.

sections.s2_technical:
A Docker image is a stack of read-only layers, and each instruction in the Dockerfile that adds files or changes the filesystem creates a layer. Docker caches these layers. On a rebuild, Docker reuses a cached layer as long as the instruction and its inputs are unchanged; the moment one layer's inputs change, that layer and every layer below it are rebuilt. This single fact drives the whole design: put instructions that rarely change near the top and instructions that change on every commit near the bottom.

A multi-stage build uses more than one `FROM`. The first stage, the builder, starts from a full JDK plus Maven, copies the source, and runs `mvn package` to produce the fat JAR. The second stage starts from a slim JRE and copies only the finished artifact out of the builder with `COPY --from=builder`. The builder stage, with its hundreds of megabytes of compiler and build tooling, is discarded; it never ships. This makes the final image dramatically smaller and reduces the attack surface because a build toolchain in production is both wasted space and extra things that can have vulnerabilities.

The layered JAR matters because a naive `COPY target/app.jar app.jar` puts your entire application — your code plus every third-party dependency — into one layer. Change one line of code, rebuild, and Docker re-downloads and re-ships the whole fat JAR including the hundred megabytes of dependencies that did not change. Spring Boot solves this with layered JARs: the fat JAR can be extracted into separate layers — `dependencies`, `spring-boot-loader`, `snapshot-dependencies`, and `application`. Your own code lives in the tiny `application` layer; the libraries live in the large `dependencies` layer. Because dependencies change far less often than your code, Docker caches the big dependency layer and only rebuilds the small application layer on a typical code change. You extract with `java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract` and then copy each layer in order in the runtime stage.

The slim JRE base image, such as a `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` or an Alpine/distroless JRE variant, contains only the Java runtime, not the compiler. You do not need `javac` in production, so shipping it is wasteful and risky. Running as a non-root user is a hard requirement in a bank: you create a dedicated user and group and switch to it with `USER`, so that if the application is compromised the attacker does not have root inside the container, which limits lateral movement and container-escape risk.

`MaxRAMPercentage` solves a subtle production bug. By default a JVM in a container can misjudge how much memory it has, and older defaults sized the heap off the host rather than the container's cgroup limit, leading to the kernel OOM-killing the container. Modern JVMs are container-aware, but you still explicitly set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` so the heap is sized as a percentage of the container's memory limit, leaving headroom for non-heap memory like metaspace, thread stacks, and native buffers. For example, with a 1 GB container limit and 75 percent, the heap maxes around 768 MB and the rest is reserved for the JVM's other needs, which prevents the container from being killed under load. The senior nuance is that you pair this with the container's actual memory limit set at deploy time, and you prefer percentage-based sizing over a fixed `-Xmx` so the same image behaves correctly whether it runs with 1 GB or 4 GB.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's team ships the account-service as a container many times a day. They hit several real problems that a production Dockerfile must solve.

Problem 1 — Every build takes forever and pushes hundreds of megabytes to the registry even when Rajesh only changed one line in a service class. The reason is the whole fat JAR, dependencies included, sits in one layer, so any code change re-ships everything. This is exactly what the layered JAR plus careful instruction order fixes: dependencies are cached in a lower layer and only the tiny application layer rebuilds.

Problem 2 — The security team scans images and flags that the production image contains a full JDK and Maven, which are not needed to run the service and expand the attack surface. This is exactly what a multi-stage build with a slim JRE runtime fixes: the toolchain stays in the discarded builder stage.

Problem 3 — The security team also flags that the container runs as root, which in a bank is unacceptable because a compromise would give root inside the container. This is exactly what creating and switching to a non-root user fixes.

Problem 4 — Under festival-season load the account-service container keeps getting OOM-killed by Kubernetes even though the host has plenty of memory. The JVM was sizing its heap wrong for the container limit. This is exactly what `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` fixes.

Because a Dockerfile is not Java, the mini-project pairs a correct production Dockerfile with a small Java demo that prints the JVM's container-aware memory decisions at startup, so you can SEE that `MaxRAMPercentage` changed the heap sizing. We build `AccountServiceApplication` with a `JvmMemoryReporter` that logs max heap, the detected container limit, and the active user, exactly the things the Dockerfile is designed to control.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the fat JAR locally (optional — the Dockerfile does this in stage 1)
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests

# Build the image using the multi-stage Dockerfile
docker build -t account-service:1.0.0 .

# Run with a 1 GB memory limit — MaxRAMPercentage=75 → heap ~768 MB
docker run --rm --memory=1g -p 8080:8080 account-service:1.0.0

# Prove the non-root user and slim image
docker run --rm account-service:1.0.0 whoami          # → bankuser (NOT root)
docker image ls account-service:1.0.0                  # → small JRE-based image

# Prove layer caching: change one service class, rebuild, and only the
# tiny application layer rebuilds — dependency layers are reused from cache.
docker build -t account-service:1.0.1 .                # fast rebuild
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the account-service source code, a `pom.xml` listing dependencies, and a deploy-time container memory limit of 1 GB.

Step 1: Docker reads the Dockerfile and starts stage 1 from a full JDK. It copies only `pom.xml` and the Maven wrapper first, then runs `dependency:go-offline`. Because `pom.xml` rarely changes, this dependency-download layer is cached and reused on most rebuilds.

Step 2: Docker copies `src/` — the thing that changes on every commit — and runs the build. This layer sits below the dependency layer, so a code change only invalidates from here down, not the expensive dependency download above.

Step 3: Stage 1 extracts the fat JAR into Spring Boot layers: a big `dependencies` layer and a tiny `application` layer, among others.

Step 4: Stage 2 starts fresh from a slim JRE. The full JDK and Maven from stage 1 are discarded and never ship. A non-root `bankuser` is created.

Step 5: Docker copies the Spring Boot layers in least-changing to most-changing order. On a typical rebuild where only code changed, the `dependencies` layer is served from cache and only the small `application` layer is rebuilt and pushed.

Step 6: The image switches to `bankuser` with `USER`, so the running process is non-root. At runtime, `docker run --memory=1g` sets the container limit; the JVM reads it and `MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` sizes the max heap to roughly 768 MB, leaving headroom.

Step 7: The application starts, and `JvmMemoryReporter` logs the chosen max heap, the container-aware processor count, and the user — confirming heap sizing and non-root both took effect.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Source code + pom.xml  ──docker build──→
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────── STAGE 1: builder (JDK + Maven) ───────────┐
  │  COPY pom.xml  ──→ layer A (deps) CACHED if unchanged  │
  │  RUN go-offline                                        │
  │  COPY src/     ──→ layer B (code) rebuilds on commit   │
  │  RUN mvn package ──→ fat JAR                            │
  │  layertools extract ──→ dependencies/ + application/   │
  └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                         │ COPY --from=builder (only artifacts)
                         ▼   (JDK + Maven DISCARDED here)
  ┌──────────── STAGE 2: runtime (slim JRE) ──────────────┐
  │  create non-root bankuser                              │
  │  COPY dependencies/     ← BIG, cached (changes rarely) │
  │  COPY spring-boot-loader/                              │
  │  COPY application/      ← TINY, rebuilt on code change │
  │  USER bankuser          ← no root in production        │
  │  ENTRYPOINT java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 ...         │
  └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                         │ docker run --memory=1g
                         ▼
  Container: heap ≈ 768 MB (75% of 1 GB), user=bankuser
           → account-service serving requests
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Production Dockerfile Design (banking) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns / Principles Used ──────────────────────┐
  │  Multi-stage build:  separate build-time vs run-time      │
  │     WHY: ship only artifacts, not the toolchain           │
  │  Layer-cache ordering: least-changing COPY first          │
  │     WHY: code change rebuilds only the tiny app layer     │
  │  Least privilege:    USER bankuser (non-root)             │
  │     WHY: bank security — contain compromise               │
  │  Resource awareness: MaxRAMPercentage over fixed -Xmx     │
  │     WHY: same image behaves correctly at 1Gi or 4Gi       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Layer Stack (bottom = base, top = most volatile) ───────

  ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │ application/  (YOUR code)       │ ← TINY, changes every commit
  ├────────────────────────────────┤
  │ snapshot-dependencies/          │ ← changes sometimes
  ├────────────────────────────────┤
  │ spring-boot-loader/             │ ← changes rarely
  ├────────────────────────────────┤
  │ dependencies/  (libraries)      │ ← BIG, changes rarely → CACHED
  ├────────────────────────────────┤
  │ bankuser + WORKDIR /app         │
  ├────────────────────────────────┤
  │ eclipse-temurin:21-jre (slim)   │ ← base, no compiler
  └────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Why instruction order matters (cache invalidation) ─────

  COPY pom.xml      → layer A   [changed? NO ] → REUSE cache
  RUN go-offline    → layer A'  [reuse]
  COPY src/         → layer B   [changed? YES] → REBUILD B and below
  RUN mvn package   → layer B'  [rebuild]
  (dependencies above B stay cached — this is the whole point)

  ── Call Chain (container startup) ─────────────────────────

  1. docker run --memory=1g account-service
  2.   → JVM reads cgroup limit = 1 GiB
  3.   → MaxRAMPercentage=75 → max heap ≈ 768 MB
  4.   → JarLauncher boots Spring context
  5.     → JvmMemoryReporter.report()
  6.       → log maxHeap, processors, user=bankuser
  7.   → account-service ready on :8080
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application is built around a multi-stage build. The first stage starts from a full JDK plus Maven, compiles the code, and produces the fat JAR; the second stage starts from a slim JRE and copies only the finished artifact out of the builder. The entire build toolchain is discarded and never ships, which makes the image much smaller and removes a compiler from production, where it is both wasted space and extra attack surface. In a bank that reduction in attack surface is not a nice-to-have, it is a requirement the security team enforces.

The layered JAR is the piece that makes rebuilds fast. If I naively copy the whole fat JAR into one layer, then changing a single line of code re-ships the entire JAR, including the hundred-plus megabytes of dependencies that did not change. Spring Boot lets me extract the fat JAR into separate layers using the layertools jarmode, which splits it into a big dependencies layer and a tiny application layer, among others. I copy those layers in the runtime stage from least-changing to most-changing, so Docker caches the large dependency layer and only rebuilds the small application layer when I change code. This is also why instruction order matters in general: a Docker image is a stack of cached layers, and any instruction whose inputs change invalidates that layer and every layer below it, so I always put the things that change least, like the pom and dependencies, before the things that change most, like my source.

For safety and correctness I run as a non-root user — I create a dedicated user and group and switch to it with USER — so a compromise does not give an attacker root inside the container. And I size memory with MaxRAMPercentage rather than a fixed Xmx. By default a JVM can misjudge how much memory it has in a container and get OOM-killed; setting MaxRAMPercentage to seventy-five means the heap is sized as a percentage of the container's memory limit, leaving headroom for metaspace, thread stacks, and native buffers, and the same image then behaves correctly whether it runs with one gigabyte or four.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this Dockerfile for our account-service. Before, every code change re-shipped the whole fat JAR and builds were slow; after the layered-JAR change, a typical code commit only rebuilt and pushed the tiny application layer and builds got dramatically faster. We moved from a JDK-based image to a slim JRE, which cleared a batch of image-scan findings, and we switched the container to a non-root user to close a security finding. The memory fix mattered most under festival-season load: our pods were being OOM-killed because the heap was sized wrong for the container limit, and moving to MaxRAMPercentage with a proper container memory limit stopped the kills entirely. Those four choices — multi-stage, layered JAR, slim non-root runtime, and percentage-based heap — are what turn a toy Dockerfile into one I am comfortable running in production in a bank.

keyPoints: Dockerfile: instructions to build an image
Multi-stage build: build in one stage, run in another — smaller image
Layer caching: order instructions for cache efficiency
COPY vs ADD: COPY is simpler and preferred
